front: Broca aphasia: lesion, speech, comprehension, repetition
back: Dominant inferior frontal gyrus (MCA superior division). Nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension and impaired repetition. Often accompanied by right face and arm weakness.

front: Wernicke aphasia: lesion and key features
back: Dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus (MCA inferior division). Fluent, paraphasic speech with poor comprehension and poor repetition. Patient is often unaware of the deficit; weakness is usually absent.
Arcuate fasciculus or supramarginal region. Fluent speech and good comprehension, but repetition is disproportionately impaired with frequent phonemic paraphasias.

front: Transcortical motor versus transcortical sensory aphasia
back: Both have intact repetition. Motor: nonfluent with good comprehension (anterior watershed). Sensory: fluent with poor comprehension (posterior watershed). Echolalia is common in the sensory type.
Large dominant perisylvian lesion, typically proximal MCA occlusion. Nonfluent speech with poor comprehension and poor repetition, usually with dense right hemiparesis.

front: Gerstmann syndrome: four findings and lesion
back: Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right left confusion. Dominant angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule.

front: Hemispatial neglect: classic lesion and features
back: Right inferior parietal lobe (nondominant) most often. Left sided inattention, extinction to double simultaneous stimulation, anosognosia, and line bisection errors toward the right.
Dominant occipital lesion plus splenium of the corpus callosum, typically left PCA infarct. Patient can write but cannot read, often with right homonymous hemianopia.
Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and oculomotor apraxia. Bilateral parieto occipital lesions, such as bilateral PCA or watershed infarcts.

front: Kluver Bucy syndrome: features and lesion
back: Bilateral anterior temporal and amygdala damage. Hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia, and hypermetamorphosis. Seen with herpes encephalitis and bilateral temporal injury.
Cortical blindness with denial of the deficit and confabulation about vision. Caused by bilateral occipital lobe damage, often bilateral PCA infarcts.

front: Alien hand syndrome: callosal versus frontal type
back: Callosal type: the nondominant hand acts against the other hand (intermanual conflict). Frontal type: dominant hand grasps and manipulates objects compulsively. Also seen in corticobasal syndrome.

front: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: findings and artery
back: Posterior inferior cerebellar or vertebral artery. Ipsilateral face pain and temperature loss, Horner, ataxia, dysphagia; contralateral body pain and temperature loss. Weakness is absent.
Anterior spinal or vertebral artery. Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face, contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception, and ipsilateral tongue weakness (hypoglossal nucleus or nerve).
Both involve the midbrain with ipsilateral third nerve palsy. Weber: contralateral hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle). Benedikt: contralateral tremor and ataxia (red nucleus) with possible hemiparesis.
Ventral pontine lesions. Millard Gubler: ipsilateral facial palsy with contralateral hemiparesis. Foville: adds ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy from involvement of the abducens nucleus or PPRF.

Medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion. Ipsilateral adduction failure on lateral gaze, with abducting nystagmus in the other eye. Convergence is spared with midbrain sparing. Think multiple sclerosis in young adults, stroke in the elderly.

Lesion of the pontine paramedian reticular formation or abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF. Ipsilateral gaze palsy and INO; the only preserved horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye.

front: Cranial nerve exits: which pass through the jugular foramen
back: Glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves (IX, X, XI). Lesions cause dysphagia, hoarseness, and shoulder weakness, as in Vernet syndrome.

front: Cavernous sinus contents and localizing finding
back: Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI, and the carotid with sympathetic fibers. Ophthalmoplegia with V1 and V2 sensory loss; the abducens is affected earliest and Horner may be present.
Inferior peduncle carries spinocerebellar and vestibular input. Middle peduncle carries pontocerebellar input only. Superior peduncle carries the main output to red nucleus and thalamus.
Vermis: truncal ataxia, titubation, gait wide based. Hemisphere: ipsilateral limb dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, and scanning dysarthria. Lesions cause ipsilateral signs.

front: Vestibulo ocular reflex: why head impulse test matters
back: A normal head impulse test with acute vertigo and nystagmus suggests a central cause (stroke). A corrective saccade on head impulse implies a peripheral lesion such as vestibular neuritis.

Saccades: contralateral frontal eye field to PPRF, ipsilateral horizontal movement. Pursuit: ipsilateral parieto occipital cortex to ipsilateral pons and cerebellum. Frontal lesions deviate gaze toward the lesion.

front: Brown Sequard syndrome: findings below a hemisection
back: Ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception (corticospinal and dorsal columns); contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few levels below (spinothalamic tract).

front: Anterior cord syndrome: spared and lost modalities
back: Loss of motor function and of pain and temperature below the lesion, with preserved vibration and position sense. Caused by anterior spinal artery infarction, as after aortic surgery.

front: Central cord syndrome: pattern and common cause
back: Arms weaker than legs with a cape like pain and temperature loss and bladder dysfunction. Typically cervical hyperextension injury in a patient with cervical spondylosis.

front: Conus medullaris versus cauda equina syndrome
back: Conus: early sphincter loss, saddle anesthesia, symmetric, mixed upper and lower motor signs, less pain. Cauda equina: asymmetric radicular pain, areflexic legs, later sphincter changes. Both need urgent MRI.

front: Subacute combined degeneration: tracts and cause
back: Dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts from vitamin B12 deficiency (or copper deficiency, nitrous oxide). Vibration loss, spastic weakness, and possible megaloblastic anemia. Treat with B12.

front: Dermatome landmarks: nipple, umbilicus, thumb, little finger
back: Nipple T4, umbilicus T10, thumb C6, middle finger C7, little finger C8, inguinal region L1, great toe L5, lateral foot S1.

front: Reflex and myotome map for C5 through S1
back: Biceps C5 and C6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, knee L3 and L4, ankle S1. Myotomes: C5 deltoid, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, L5 dorsiflexion, S1 plantar flexion.

front: Upper trunk versus lower trunk brachial plexopathy
back: Upper trunk (Erb): shoulder abduction and elbow flexion weakness, waiter's tip posture. Lower trunk (Klumpke): hand intrinsic weakness, C8 and T1 sensory loss, and possible Horner syndrome.
Second order neurons cross in the anterior white commissure within a few segments of entry. Dorsal column fibers cross later in the medulla as the medial lemniscus.
Anterior communicating, anterior cerebral, internal carotid, posterior communicating, posterior cerebral, and basilar tip. Berry aneurysms occur most often at the anterior communicating junction.

Anterior watershed between ACA and MCA causes proximal arm and leg weakness (man in a barrel). Posterior watershed between MCA and PCA causes visual and parietal deficits. Cause is systemic hypotension.

front: Artery of Percheron and anterior choroidal artery
back: Percheron: single trunk to bilateral paramedian thalami, causing vertical gaze palsy, hypersomnolence, and amnesia. Anterior choroidal: contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and hemianopia.

front: MRI choice: acute ischemia, hemorrhage, and demyelination
back: Diffusion weighted imaging (with low ADC) detects acute infarct within minutes. Susceptibility weighted imaging shows microbleeds and blood. FLAIR highlights periventricular demyelinating plaques and edema.

Avoid group 1 agents in severe kidney disease (eGFR under 30) because of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Gadolinium crosses the placenta, so avoid in pregnancy unless essential. Brain deposition has been described.

Vasogenic edema (high ADC) in parieto occipital white matter on FLAIR, with hypertension, eclampsia, or immunosuppressants such as tacrolimus. Usually reversible with blood pressure control and stopping the trigger.

front: Noncontrast head CT: first test for which problems
back: Acute hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus, and skull fracture. Hyperacute blood appears bright; early ischemia may be invisible. Choose CT in unstable patients and when MRI is unavailable.

FDG PET shows regional hypometabolism: temporal in Alzheimer disease, interictal focus in epilepsy surgery planning. DaT SPECT shows reduced striatal dopamine transporter binding in Parkinson disease, not in essential tremor.

Mass lesion with shift, obstructive hydrocephalus, coagulopathy, platelet count under 50,000, and skin infection at the site. Image first when papilledema, focal deficit, or altered consciousness is present.

front: CSF in bacterial versus viral versus fungal meningitis
back: Bacterial: neutrophils, protein high, glucose low. Viral: lymphocytes, protein mildly high, glucose normal. Fungal or tuberculous: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose, with elevated opening pressure in cryptococcus.
Elevated CSF protein with normal white cell count. Classic for Guillain Barre syndrome after the first week. Also seen with spinal block and CIDP.

Bands present in CSF but not matched in serum indicate intrathecal IgG synthesis. Found in over 90 percent of multiple sclerosis cases but are not specific; also seen in neurosyphilis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

front: Normal opening pressure and high pressure causes
back: Normal adult opening pressure is up to 25 cm of water in the lateral decubitus position. Elevation suggests idiopathic intracranial hypertension, venous sinus thrombosis, or cryptococcal meningitis.

front: Post lumbar puncture headache: features and treatment
back: Orthostatic headache within five days, worse upright and relieved lying down. Treat with fluids, caffeine, and rest; persistent cases need an epidural blood patch. Atraumatic needles lower the risk.

front: Xanthochromia and the timing of SAH testing
back: Yellow CSF supernatant from bilirubin appears about 6 to 12 hours after subarachnoid bleeding and persists for weeks. Spectrophotometry separates true bleeding from traumatic tap.

front: Uncal versus central versus subfalcine herniation
back: Uncal: ipsilateral dilated pupil, then hemiparesis (Kernohan notch is false localizing). Central: downward diencephalic displacement with declining consciousness. Subfalcine: cingulate shift beneath the falx, possibly compressing the ACA.
Mannitol 0.25 to 1 g per kg or hypertonic saline (for example 23.4 percent bolus). Keep serum sodium under 160 and osmolality under 320 as limits. Hyperventilation is a brief bridge only.

Lowers PaCO2 to 30 to 35 mm Hg and causes vasoconstriction, giving rapid but short lived pressure reduction. Prolonged use risks cerebral ischemia, so use only as a temporary bridge to definitive therapy.

Known irreversible cause, no confounders (sedatives, hypothermia, shock, metabolic derangement), coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea with PaCO2 at least 60 mm Hg or 20 above baseline. Ancillary tests only when apnea testing cannot be done.

front: Spinal reflexes that may persist in brain death
back: Triple flexion, Lazarus sign, deep tendon reflexes, and plantar responses can occur. Absent: pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, vestibulo ocular, gag, and cough reflexes, plus spontaneous respiration.

front: Targeted temperature management after cardiac arrest
back: Comatose survivors need temperature control (avoid fever, often 32 to 37.5 degrees Celsius). Prognosticate no earlier than 72 hours after normothermia with multimodal evidence such as bilateral absent N20, MRI, and EEG.

Forced vital capacity under 20 mL per kg, maximal inspiratory pressure weaker than minus 30 cm of water, or maximal expiratory pressure under 40 signal impending failure. Intubate early and watch autonomic instability.

front: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
back: Serotonin: rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea; treat with cyproheptadine. NMS: days of dopamine blockade, lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high creatine kinase; treat with dantrolene or bromocriptine.

front: Enzyme inducers and inhibitors among antiseizure drugs
back: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and primidone induce CYP3A4 and lower oral contraceptive levels. Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and raises lamotrigine levels, so halve the lamotrigine dose.

Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects and lower IQ. Give folic acid daily before conception. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest malformation risk, but lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy.

Sensitivity is true positives over all with disease (rules out when high). Specificity is true negatives over all without disease (rules in when high). Predictive values change with disease prevalence.

front: Capacity assessment elements and surrogate order
back: Capacity needs understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a stable choice, and is decision specific. If absent, use an advance directive, then a health care proxy, then family by statute. Disclose errors promptly and honestly.

front: TOAST classification of ischemic stroke: five categories
back: Large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small vessel occlusion (lacunar), stroke of other determined etiology (dissection, hypercoagulable state), and stroke of undetermined etiology (cryptogenic, two causes, or incomplete workup).

front: Pure motor hemiparesis lacune: usual site
back: Posterior limb of the internal capsule or basis pontis. Face, arm, and leg weakness with no cortical signs, sensory loss, or visual loss. Caused by lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries from hypertension.
Ventral posterolateral thalamic lacune producing hemisensory loss of face, arm, and leg without weakness. A later central pain (thalamic pain) syndrome can follow weeks to months afterward.

front: Ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria clumsy hand syndrome
back: Lacunar syndromes from the basis pontis or internal capsule. Ataxic hemiparesis: weakness plus ipsilateral ataxia out of proportion. Dysarthria clumsy hand: facial weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia, and a clumsy hand.

front: MCA stem occlusion versus superior division versus inferior division
back: Stem: contralateral hemiplegia, hemisensory loss, gaze deviation toward lesion, aphasia or neglect. Superior division: motor, Broca aphasia. Inferior division: Wernicke aphasia, superior quadrantanopia or neglect, little weakness.

Contralateral leg weakness greater than arm, abulia, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex, and transcortical motor aphasia if left sided. Bilateral ACA infarcts from a shared A1 produce akinetic mutism.

Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, alexia without agraphia if left occipital plus splenium, and memory loss with bilateral medial temporal involvement. Thalamic branches cause hemisensory loss and thalamic pain.

Embolic occlusion at the basilar apex causing bilateral thalamic and midbrain ischemia: vertical gaze palsy, pupillary abnormalities, somnolence, peduncular hallucinosis, and memory loss. Cortical blindness occurs from occipital involvement.

front: Locked in syndrome: lesion and preserved function
back: Ventral pontine infarct from basilar occlusion. Quadriplegia and anarthria with intact consciousness. Vertical eye movements and blinking are preserved because the tectal and midbrain pathways are spared. EEG is normal.

front: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: vessel and findings
back: Vertebral or PICA occlusion. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, facial pain and temperature loss, ataxia, and bulbar weakness. Contralateral body pain and temperature loss. Vertigo, hiccups, and dysphagia are common.

front: Cerebellar infarct with brainstem compression: next step
back: Worsening drowsiness, headache, and vomiting after a large cerebellar infarct signal edema and hydrocephalus. Urgent posterior fossa decompression with or without ventricular drain is lifesaving, even before neurologic collapse.

front: CHA2DS2 VASc score components and anticoagulation threshold
back: Heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or older 2, diabetes 1, prior stroke or TIA 2, vascular disease 1, age 65 to 74 1, female sex 1. Anticoagulate at 2 or more for men, 3 or more for women.

front: Anticoagulant choice in atrial fibrillation with a mechanical valve or moderate to severe mitral stenosis
back: Use warfarin with a target INR (2.5 to 3.5 for most mechanical mitral valves). Direct oral anticoagulants are inferior or harmful in this setting and are not recommended.

front: Timing of DOAC start after AF related ischemic stroke
back: Recent trial evidence supports early initiation, within about 48 hours for minor or moderate strokes and around day 6 to 7 for large infarcts, individualized by infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk.

Prolonged rhythm monitoring with an implantable loop recorder detects occult atrial fibrillation far more often than 24 hour Holter. Recommended for cryptogenic stroke after a standard workup, especially in older patients.

Consider closure in patients aged 18 to 60 with a cryptogenic embolic infarct, no other cause found, and a PFO with high risk features (atrial septal aneurysm or large shunt). Antiplatelet therapy is the alternative.

front: Infective endocarditis and ischemic stroke: avoid which therapy
back: Do not give thrombolysis (high hemorrhage and mycotic aneurysm risk). Anticoagulation is generally avoided too. Treat with prolonged antibiotics and early valve surgery when indicated. Obtain vascular imaging for mycotic aneurysm.

front: Left ventricular thrombus after anterior myocardial infarction
back: Embolic stroke risk is high. Treat with anticoagulation, usually warfarin or a DOAC, for about three months with repeat imaging. Anteroapical akinesis and low ejection fraction are the predisposing features.

front: NIHSS: maximum score and what it undermeasures
back: Maximum 42. It weights left hemisphere deficits more than right (language counts more than neglect) and underrates posterior circulation strokes causing vertigo, ataxia, or diplopia.

Alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of last known well. Beyond 4.5 hours, selected patients with a DWI FLAIR mismatch (wake up stroke) or perfusion mismatch on advanced imaging may still be treated.
Before treatment lower to below 185 over 110. After treatment keep below 180 over 105 for at least 24 hours. If untreated, permissive hypertension up to 220 over 120 is acceptable.

Any intracranial hemorrhage on CT, extensive hypodensity, recent major head trauma or intracranial surgery within 3 months, known intracranial neoplasm or AVM with bleeding risk, active internal bleeding, and platelets under 100,000.

front: Thrombectomy criteria for anterior circulation LVO
back: Occlusion of the internal carotid or proximal MCA (M1), NIHSS 6 or more, ASPECTS 6 or more, pre stroke independence. Treat within 6 hours, or up to 24 hours with favorable perfusion or clinical imaging mismatch.

Recent trials show benefit in selected patients with ASPECTS 3 to 5 or large perfusion cores, improving functional outcome despite higher symptomatic hemorrhage rates. Patient selection and goals of care still matter.

Hypoglycemia (check glucose first), postictal Todd paralysis, complicated migraine, conversion disorder, and hemiplegic syndromes. Treat suspected stroke only after glucose is confirmed above 50 mg/dL.

Putamen most common, then thalamus, pons, cerebellum, and deep white matter. Lobar hemorrhage in older adults suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy, with microbleeds on SWI and apolipoprotein E e4 or e2 association.

front: Reversal of warfarin related intracerebral hemorrhage
back: Four factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg. Fresh frozen plasma is slower and volume heavy. Target INR below 1.4 quickly.

front: Reversal of dabigatran versus factor Xa inhibitors
back: Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Apixaban and rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa, or four factor prothrombin complex concentrate if unavailable. Time since last dose guides urgency.

front: Blood pressure goal in acute intracerebral hemorrhage
back: For presenting systolic pressure of 150 to 220 mmHg, lowering to around 140 is safe and may improve outcome. Avoid dropping below 130. Use nicardipine or labetalol infusion with close monitoring.

Cerebellar hemorrhage over 3 cm with neurologic decline, brainstem compression, or hydrocephalus needs urgent evacuation. Supratentorial surgery is considered for deteriorating lobar clots near the surface. Deep clots rarely benefit.

front: Subarachnoid hemorrhage: first test and next step
back: Noncontrast CT within 6 hours has near perfect sensitivity. If negative and suspicion remains, perform lumbar puncture for xanthochromia. Then CT angiography or catheter angiography to find the aneurysm.

front: Vasospasm timing and treatment after SAH
back: Peaks 4 to 14 days after bleed. Give nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours) from admission to improve outcome, maintain euvolemia, and treat symptomatic spasm with induced hypertension or endovascular therapy.
Usually cerebral salt wasting with volume depletion, not SIADH. Treat with isotonic saline and fludrocortisone. Fluid restriction worsens vasospasm risk.

front: Hunt and Hess versus WFNS grading
back: Both grade SAH severity. Hunt and Hess runs 1 to 5 by headache, nuchal rigidity, deficit, and coma. WFNS uses Glasgow Coma Scale plus motor deficit. Poor grade means worse prognosis.

Symptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99 percent: endarterectomy within 2 weeks. Symptomatic 50 to 69 percent: consider in selected men. Asymptomatic over 60 percent: consider only with low surgical risk and long life expectancy.

front: Pure sensory seizure aura versus hallucinated smell
back: A recurrent unpleasant odor aura points to the uncus and mesial temporal lobe. Rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, and fear suggest mesial temporal onset.

front: Cervical artery dissection: presentation and treatment
back: Neck or face pain, partial Horner syndrome, and ischemic events in a younger patient. Confirm with CT or MR angiography. Treat with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for 3 to 6 months.

front: Antiplatelet choice after minor stroke or high risk TIA
back: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel started within 24 hours for 21 days, then single agent. Longer combination increases bleeding without added benefit.

front: Cerebral venous thrombosis: presentation and treatment
back: Headache, seizures, papilledema, and venous infarcts crossing arterial territories, often with hemorrhage. MR venography confirms. Anticoagulate even with hemorrhage, using warfarin or DOAC after initial parenteral therapy.

RCVS: thunderclap headaches, reversible beaded vessels over weeks, normal CSF, triggered by vasoactive drugs or postpartum. PACNS: subacute headache, abnormal CSF, brain biopsy, treated with steroids and cyclophosphamide.

Age over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, or visual loss: start high dose prednisone at once before biopsy. Elevated ESR and CRP support the diagnosis. Temporal artery biopsy remains confirmatory.

Young patients with large MCA infarcts and edema may benefit from decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours, reducing mortality and improving survival with disability. Benefit is smaller above age 60.
Classify by awareness (aware or impaired awareness), then onset (motor or nonmotor), then evolution to bilateral tonic clonic. Replaces the terms simple partial and complex partial.

Oral and manual automatisms with impaired awareness suggest temporal lobe onset. Unilateral hand automatism is ipsilateral, with contralateral dystonic posturing. Postictal aphasia suggests dominant hemisphere onset.

Brief, stereotyped nocturnal events with bizarre hypermotor posturing, bicycling, and rapid recovery without confusion. Often misread as psychogenic events or parasomnia. Scalp EEG is frequently normal.

Long duration, eye closure during event, asynchronous thrashing, pelvic thrusting, crying afterward, and memory preserved. Tongue bite at the tip, normal prolactin, and video EEG without ictal discharge support the diagnosis.
Syncope: prodrome of lightheadedness, brief jerks under 15 seconds, rapid recovery, pallor. Seizure: aura, prolonged tonic clonic phase, lateral tongue bite, postictal confusion, and incontinence.
Alpha at 8 to 13 Hz over occipital regions with eyes closed, attenuating with eye opening. A slow posterior rhythm in an adult is abnormal.

Typical of childhood absence epilepsy, triggered by hyperventilation. Faster 4 to 6 Hz polyspike and wave suggests juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Slow 2.5 Hz spike and wave suggests Lennox Gastaut syndrome.

front: Hypsarrhythmia EEG pattern and its syndrome
back: Chaotic, high voltage, disorganized background with multifocal spikes seen in infantile spasms (West syndrome). Treat urgently with ACTH, prednisolone, or vigabatrin (first line in tuberous sclerosis).
Frontally predominant generalized waves with anterior to posterior lag, seen in hepatic and other metabolic encephalopathies. Can be mistaken for periodic discharges.

Alternating high voltage bursts and flat suppression. Seen under deep anesthesia or barbiturates, after severe anoxic injury, and in early infantile developmental epileptic encephalopathies such as Ohtahara syndrome.
Periodic sharp waves over one hemisphere repeating every 1 to 2 seconds. Classically seen in herpes simplex encephalitis, acute stroke, and tumors, and associated with seizures.
High resolution thin cut T1, T2, and FLAIR with coronal angulation perpendicular to the hippocampus at 3 tesla. Looks for hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, tumors, and malformations.

front: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: features and drug choice
back: Adolescent morning myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic clonic seizures, and absence, with sleep deprivation as trigger. Valproate is most effective, but avoid in women of childbearing age. Lamotrigine or levetiracetam are alternatives. Lifelong therapy is usual.
Ethosuximide is first line when absence is the only seizure type. Valproate is better if generalized tonic clonic seizures coexist. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence.

front: Dravet syndrome: gene and drugs to avoid
back: SCN1A mutation with febrile prolonged seizures in infancy and later developmental decline. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin) worsen seizures. Use valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, or fenfluramine.

Multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic), cognitive impairment, and slow spike and wave with paroxysmal fast activity during sleep. Treat with valproate, lamotrigine, rufinamide, clobazam, or cannabidiol. Felbamate is a last resort.

front: Self limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
back: Child aged 4 to 10 with nocturnal facial twitching, drooling, and speech arrest, with centrotemporal spikes. Often needs no treatment and remits by adolescence.

front: Carbamazepine adverse effects and HLA testing
back: Hyponatremia, rash, aplastic anemia, enzyme induction. HLA B*1502 in patients of Asian ancestry predicts Stevens Johnson syndrome and requires testing before starting.
Teratogenic (neural tube defects, lower IQ), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, tremor, weight gain, thrombocytopenia, and hyperammonemia. Avoid in mitochondrial disease (POLG mutations).

front: Antiseizure drugs that worsen generalized epilepsies
back: Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, and gabapentin or pregabalin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures. Prefer valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or ethosuximide in generalized syndromes.

front: Enzyme inducing antiseizure drugs and contraception
back: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, and topiramate at high dose reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Lamotrigine levels fall with estrogen, so doses need adjustment.

At 5 minutes give a benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.1 mg per kg IV, midazolam IM, or diazepam). Then a second line agent: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate. Refractory cases need anesthetic infusion with EEG monitoring.
Ages 6 months to 5 years with fever and no CNS infection. Simple febrile seizures are brief and generalized, with no need for antiseizure drugs or neuroimaging. Recurrence risk is about 30 percent.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate is first line, superior to benzodiazepines or phenytoin. Delivery and blood pressure control follow. Watch for loss of reflexes as sign of magnesium toxicity.

Anterior temporal lobectomy for drug resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy yields seizure freedom in about 60 to 70 percent, far better than continued medication. Failure of two appropriate drugs defines drug resistance.

front: Vagus nerve stimulation versus responsive neurostimulation
back: VNS is palliative, reduces seizures by about half over time, with hoarseness as common adverse effect. RNS records and stimulates at the seizure focus and suits one or two defined foci not resectable.
Frequent generalized tonic clonic seizures, nocturnal seizures, and poor adherence raise risk. Best prevention is seizure control, adherence, and nighttime supervision where possible.
Sudden anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning for under 24 hours, preserved identity, and no other deficits. Often follows exertion or emotional stress. Benign, with low recurrence.

front: Conduction block versus temporal dispersion: why does it matter?
back: Conduction block (amplitude drop of proximal versus distal CMAP, area also falls) implies focal demyelination, as in acquired demyelinating neuropathy. Temporal dispersion widens the CMAP with preserved area. Block at a non entrapment site suggests CIDP or MMN.

front: Axonal versus demyelinating neuropathy on nerve conduction studies
back: Axonal loss: low amplitudes, relatively preserved velocity and latency, and fibrillation potentials on EMG. Demyelination: markedly slowed velocities, prolonged distal latencies and F waves, conduction block, and dispersion, with amplitudes relatively preserved.

front: Sensory NAP normal in a patient with numb hand and radicular pain
back: Preganglionic lesion (radiculopathy) spares the dorsal root ganglion, so the sensory nerve action potential stays normal despite sensory loss. An absent SNAP in the numb dermatome points to a plexus or nerve lesion, distal to the ganglion.

front: F wave and H reflex: what do they test?
back: F waves are late responses from antidromic motor axon activation, useful for proximal motor segments such as roots and plexus. The H reflex is the electrical analog of the ankle jerk (S1 pathway); absent H reflex suggests S1 radiculopathy or polyneuropathy.

front: Needle EMG: neuropathic versus myopathic motor unit potentials
back: Neuropathic: large, long, polyphasic units with reduced recruitment and early fibrillations after about 2 to 3 weeks. Myopathic: small, short, polyphasic units with early full recruitment. Irritability can also appear in inflammatory myopathy.

front: First test in suspected length dependent distal symmetric polyneuropathy
back: Fasting glucose or glucose tolerance, vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid, and serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation are the highest yield screens. Add TSH, renal function, and medication and toxin review as indicated.

Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal column loss (vibratory and position sense), corticospinal signs, and sensory axonal neuropathy with possible cognitive change. Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; T2 hyperintensity in the posterior cervical cord; treat with parenteral B12.

front: Copper deficiency myeloneuropathy: classic causes and mimic
back: Mimics B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia and spasticity, plus anemia and neutropenia. Causes include bariatric surgery, excess zinc intake (including denture cream), and malabsorption. Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin; treat with copper replacement.

Both cause neuropathy. Deficiency follows isoniazid, hydralazine, and malnutrition. Excess megadoses cause a pure sensory neuronopathy with ataxia. Prevent isoniazid neuropathy with supplemental pyridoxine; stop the excess source in toxicity.

front: Small fiber neuropathy: how is it diagnosed?
back: Burning pain, allodynia, and autonomic symptoms with normal strength, reflexes, and nerve conduction studies. Diagnose by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy or abnormal autonomic testing. Check glucose tolerance, since impaired tolerance is common.

front: Hereditary transthyretin amyloid neuropathy: features and therapy
back: Length dependent sensorimotor and early autonomic neuropathy with carpal tunnel, cardiomyopathy, and weight loss. Autosomal dominant TTR variants. Treatments: TTR silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) and stabilizers such as tafamidis.

front: AL amyloid neuropathy: key associations and tests
back: Painful small fiber and autonomic neuropathy with carpal tunnel, macroglossia, orthostasis, and nephrotic syndrome from clonal plasma cell disease. Check serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains; confirm with tissue (fat pad or nerve) Congo red staining.

Painful, stepwise, asymmetric multiple mononeuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) with axonal loss, often with systemic features. Confirm with nerve and muscle biopsy. Treat with high dose glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide for systemic disease, or rituximab.

front: Paraproteinemic neuropathy: IgM versus IgG or IgA
back: IgM with anti MAG antibodies gives slowly progressive distal demyelinating sensory ataxic neuropathy with tremor and disproportionately prolonged distal latencies. IgG or IgA monoclonal gammopathy raises concern for CIDP or POEMS. Always exclude amyloid.

front: Charcot Marie Tooth 1A: genetics and findings
back: PMP22 duplication, autosomal dominant. Uniform slowing of median motor velocity below about 38 m/s, pes cavus, hammer toes, distal atrophy (stork legs), onion bulb pathology. Avoid vincristine, which can precipitate severe neuropathy.

Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies from PMP22 deletion. Recurrent painless focal mononeuropathies after compression or minor trauma. Studies show focal slowing at entrapment sites with a mild diffuse background demyelination.

front: CMT X1 and CMT2A: gene and pattern
back: CMTX1 is GJB1 (connexin 32), X linked, with intermediate velocities and men more severely affected than women. CMT2A is MFN2, the most common axonal form, with early onset severe disease. Both are common exam associations.

front: Diabetic neuropathy variants beyond distal polyneuropathy
back: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (amyotrophy): painful thigh weakness with weight loss. Also truncal radiculopathy, cranial mononeuropathy such as CN III with pupil sparing, and autonomic neuropathy. Treat glycemia and pain, not with routine immunotherapy.

Prolonged median distal sensory and motor latencies across the wrist, with a sensory change first. Comparing median to ulnar or radial sensory latencies in the same hand increases sensitivity. Severe cases show thenar denervation. Treat with a night splint, steroid injection, or release.

front: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow: localization and findings
back: Slowing of conduction velocity across the elbow (below about 50 m/s) or a drop in amplitude with focal block. Splits in sensation spare the dorsal forearm. Dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory involvement places the lesion proximal to the wrist.

front: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove versus posterior cord
back: Spiral groove lesion causes wrist and finger drop with triceps sparing and preserved sensation, except a dorsal hand patch. Posterior cord lesion also involves deltoid and triceps. Posterior interosseous lesion spares sensation and brachioradialis.

front: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
back: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion, and sensory loss on the lateral shin and dorsum of the foot. Inversion and hip abduction are spared, unlike L5 radiculopathy. Sciatic peroneal division lesion also spares tibialis posterior if purely peroneal.

front: L5 versus common peroneal lesion: the discriminating muscles
back: Weak foot inversion (tibialis posterior) and weak hip abduction (gluteus medius) point to L5 radiculopathy, since the common peroneal nerve does not supply them. Paraspinal EMG abnormalities also favor radiculopathy.

Abrupt severe shoulder pain, then patchy weakness of upper trunk muscles, sometimes after infection, surgery, or vaccination. Immune mediated, with recurrent or hereditary forms linked to SEPT9. Management is analgesia and rehabilitation; short steroid courses early are sometimes used.

front: True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome: classic findings
back: Hand wasting with thenar predominance (Gilliatt Sumner hand), medial forearm sensory loss, low median motor and ulnar sensory amplitudes, often from a cervical rib or fibrous band at C8 to T1 trunk. Treat with surgical decompression.

Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy, retroperitoneal hematoma (especially anticoagulated patients), malignant infiltration, and radiation. Painless slowly progressive weakness suggests radiation, while sudden painful thigh weakness after an anticoagulant suggests hematoma.

Progressive symmetric weakness with areflexia over days to 4 weeks after infection such as Campylobacter jejuni. CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation. Nadir within 4 weeks. Early studies may be normal; low velocities and absent F waves appear first.

Plasma exchange (about 5 sessions) or IVIG 2 g per kg over 5 days, started in patients who cannot walk unaided within 4 weeks of onset. Steroids are not effective. Combining both therapies adds nothing; monitor forced vital capacity and autonomic instability.

front: Guillain Barre variants: AMAN, AIDP, pharyngeal cervical brachial
back: AIDP is the demyelinating form in Western countries. AMAN is axonal motor, linked to GM1 antibodies and Campylobacter. Pharyngeal cervical brachial variant causes oropharyngeal and arm weakness with GT1a antibodies. Bickerstaff has encephalopathy added.

front: Miller Fisher syndrome triad and antibody
back: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, with anti GQ1b antibodies. Treat like Guillain Barre syndrome, though many recover spontaneously. Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis overlaps and also carries anti GQ1b antibodies with drowsiness or hyperreflexia.

Progressive or relapsing symmetric proximal and distal weakness over more than 8 weeks with demyelinating conduction studies and elevated CSF protein. Treat with steroids, IVIG, or plasma exchange; maintenance with subcutaneous immunoglobulin is an option.

front: Nodopathy with anti neurofascin or contactin antibodies
back: Often presents as CIDP like disease that responds poorly to IVIG, with tremor, ataxia, or nephrotic syndrome (contactin or CASPR). IgG4 antibodies. Rituximab is commonly effective, and antibody testing guides the choice of therapy.

front: Multifocal motor neuropathy: features and treatment
back: Asymmetric distal arm weakness with conduction block in motor nerves, no sensory loss, and anti GM1 IgM antibodies in some patients. Fasciculations and cramps can mimic ALS. IVIG is first line; steroids and plasma exchange are ineffective or can worsen it.

Polyneuropathy (demyelinating, painful), organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M protein (usually lambda), and skin changes, with VEGF elevation and sclerotic bone lesions. Treat solitary lesions with radiation and disseminated disease with chemotherapy or autologous stem cell transplantation.

front: Lyme neuroborreliosis: neuropathy pattern and treatment
back: Cranial neuropathy (often bilateral facial palsy), radiculoneuritis with pain, and lymphocytic meningitis. Treat with oral doxycycline for isolated facial palsy, or intravenous ceftriaxone for meningitis and radiculopathy. Test serum antibodies with confirmatory immunoblot.

front: MELAS: genetics, features, and drugs to avoid
back: Mitochondrial DNA m.3243A to G mutation: stroke like episodes not in vascular territories, lactic acidosis, seizures, diabetes, and hearing loss, with ragged red fibers on biopsy. Avoid valproate and metformin; consider arginine for acute episodes.

front: ALS: Awaji and El Escorial diagnostic principle
back: Upper and lower motor neuron signs progressing within body regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbar), with EMG evidence of active and chronic denervation in clinically unaffected regions, and exclusion of mimics. Sensation and sphincters are typically spared.

front: ALS genetics and gene directed therapy
back: C9orf72 repeat expansion is the most common familial cause (also frontotemporal dementia). SOD1 and FUS are others. Tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide given intrathecally, is approved for SOD1 related ALS.

front: ALS disease modifying and supportive management
back: Riluzole (glutamate modulator) modestly prolongs survival; edaravone slows functional decline in selected patients. Noninvasive ventilation extends survival once FVC falls or orthopnea appears; offer gastrostomy before FVC drops below about 50 percent.

front: Primary lateral sclerosis versus progressive muscular atrophy
back: PLS is pure upper motor neuron disease with spasticity and pseudobulbar signs and a slower course. PMA is pure lower motor neuron disease. Either may later evolve into ALS, so serial examination is required.

X linked bulbospinal muscular atrophy from CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene. Men have proximal weakness, bulbar fasciculations, gynecomastia, tremor, and sensory neuropathy. Elevated creatine kinase; slower course than ALS.

front: Spinal muscular atrophy: gene and treatments
back: Autosomal recessive SMN1 deletion; severity is modified by SMN2 copy number. Floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and areflexia. Treatments: nusinersen intrathecally, risdiplam orally, and onasemnogene gene therapy, most effective when started early.

Hypokalemic (CACNA1S or SCN4A): attacks after carbohydrate loads or rest following exercise; treat with potassium. Hyperkalemic (SCN4A): brief attacks with myotonia after rest or potassium; treat with carbohydrates, thiazides, or acetazolamide. Thyrotoxic form occurs in Asian men.

SPG4 (SPAST) is the most common autosomal dominant form, a pure form with slowly progressive leg spasticity and little weakness. Brain and spinal cord imaging is typically unrevealing. Treat with baclofen, stretching, and physiotherapy.

Prednisolone started within 72 hours improves recovery; antivirals add little alone and may help in severe cases combined with steroids. Protect the eye with lubrication and taping. Most patients recover substantially within months.

front: Ramsay Hunt syndrome versus Bell palsy
back: Varicella zoster reactivation of the geniculate ganglion causes facial palsy with ear pain and vesicles in the ear canal or palate, sometimes with hearing loss and vertigo. Prognosis is worse. Treat with prednisone plus an antiviral such as valacyclovir.

Dorsal root ganglion loss gives asymmetric patchy sensory ataxia with absent SNAPs and pseudoathetosis. Causes: Sjogren syndrome, anti Hu paraneoplastic disease (small cell lung cancer), cisplatin, and pyridoxine excess. Motor strength is preserved.

Myalgia with or without CK rise is common; rhabdomyolysis is rare. Persistent weakness after stopping the drug with high CK suggests immune mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti HMGCR antibodies. Check TSH and vitamin D, and consider lower dose or alternative agent.

front: Myasthenia gravis antibody profile by phenotype
back: AChR antibodies in most generalized disease and thymoma association. MuSK antibodies: young women, bulbar, neck, and respiratory weakness, poor response to pyridostigmine, and thymus not involved. LRP4 is a minority; some patients are seronegative.

Indicated for any thymoma. In AChR positive generalized disease younger than about 65 years, thymectomy improves outcomes and reduces steroid need. It is not routinely recommended for MuSK positive disease or purely ocular myasthenia.

Pyridostigmine first, then prednisone for moderate disease, with steroid sparing agents such as azathioprine, mycophenolate, or methotrexate. Refractory cases: rituximab (especially MuSK), complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab) for AChR positive, or FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab).

Respiratory failure from weakness. Intubate or use noninvasive ventilation when FVC is below about 20 mL per kg or NIF is weaker than about negative 30. Treat with plasma exchange or IVIG, hold pyridostigmine temporarily, and search for infection or provoking drugs.

Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, magnesium, beta blockers, and botulinum toxin. Checkpoint inhibitors can also induce myasthenia. Corticosteroids can cause early transient worsening, so start low or give with plasma exchange or IVIG cover.

Transient neonatal myasthenia from maternal IgG crossing the placenta causes hypotonia and weak feeding for weeks. Manage pregnancy with pyridostigmine and prednisone; avoid mycophenolate (teratogenic) and avoid magnesium for eclampsia in myasthenic patients when possible.

front: Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome features and treatment
back: Presynaptic P/Q voltage gated calcium channel antibodies. Proximal weakness, hyporeflexia improving after exercise, dry mouth, and impotence. Half have small cell lung cancer. Treat with 3,4 diaminopyridine (amifampridine), then immunotherapy and cancer care.

front: Repetitive stimulation: myasthenia gravis versus Lambert Eaton
back: Myasthenia: low baseline CMAP and decrement of more than 10 percent at 2 to 3 Hz, improving after brief exercise. Lambert Eaton: low CMAP, decrement at low rate, but increment more than 100 percent after brief exercise or at 20 to 50 Hz.

Presynaptic toxin blocks acetylcholine release: descending paralysis with dilated pupils, ptosis, and dry mouth. Infant botulism from spores (honey) causes constipation and hypotonia. Give antitoxin promptly (BabyBIG for infants) and supportive ventilation; avoid aminoglycosides.

Tick paralysis: ascending flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain Barre, reversed by finding and removing the engorged tick. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase causing a cholinergic crisis; treat with atropine and pralidoxime. Both can produce abnormal repetitive stimulation.

front: Congenital myasthenic syndromes: clues and treatment caution
back: Onset in infancy or childhood with fatigable weakness and no antibodies, often a decremental response. Treatment depends on gene: CHRNE responds to pyridostigmine, 3,4 diaminopyridine, or salbutamol, while DOK7 and slow channel syndromes worsen with pyridostigmine.

front: Duchenne muscular dystrophy: genetics and course
back: X linked recessive DMD mutations with absent dystrophin, usually frame shift deletions. Boys have calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, markedly high CK, and loss of ambulation by early teen years. Dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure follow.

front: Duchenne treatment: steroids, exon skipping, gene therapy
back: Glucocorticoids (prednisone or deflazacort) prolong ambulation. Exon skipping (eteplirsen, golodirsen) applies to amenable deletions, and micro dystrophin gene therapy to eligible boys. Monitor cardiac function, bone health, and respiratory status.

front: McArdle disease: enzyme, features, and test
back: Myophosphorylase deficiency (glycogen storage type V). Exercise intolerance with cramps, the second wind phenomenon, and myoglobinuria. Forearm ischemic exercise shows no lactate rise with exaggerated ammonia rise; CK is elevated at rest.

D4Z4 repeat contraction on chromosome 4q35 (FSHD1) with DUX4 expression. Facial weakness, scapular winging, and asymmetric humeral and foot dorsiflexor weakness with sparing of deltoid. Retinal telangiectasia and hearing loss can occur.

DM1: CTG expansion in DMPK, distal and facial weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction disease, and anticipation. DM2: CCTG expansion in CNBP with proximal weakness, myalgia, and less severe disease. Obtain ECG surveillance in both.

Early contractures of elbows, Achilles tendons, and spine with humeroperoneal weakness, from emerin (X linked) or lamin A/C mutations. Cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmia require pacemaker or defibrillator evaluation and regular cardiac screening.

Acid alpha glucosidase deficiency with vacuolar myopathy. Adult onset proximal and respiratory weakness with elevated CK; dried blood spot enzyme assay confirms. Treat with enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa, avalglucosidase alfa); diaphragm weakness may cause early hypoventilation.

front: Central core disease and malignant hyperthermia
back: RYR1 mutation causes congenital myopathy with central cores on oxidative stains and substantial risk of malignant hyperthermia. Avoid volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine; treat crisis with dantrolene. Use a trigger free anesthetic.

front: Dermatomyositis: skin signs, antibodies, and malignancy
back: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and perifascicular atrophy on biopsy. Anti Mi 2 carries classic skin disease; anti TIF1 gamma and NXP2 raise cancer risk in adults, so screen for malignancy. Anti MDA5 links to interstitial lung disease.

Subacute severe proximal weakness with very high CK, necrotic fibers with little inflammation. Antibodies against SRP or HMGCR (statin exposed). Treat with immunotherapy such as steroids, IVIG, or rituximab; stop the statin.

front: Inclusion body myositis: pattern and therapy
back: Age above 50 with slowly progressive finger flexor and quadriceps weakness and dysphagia, mildly raised CK, rimmed vacuoles, and endomysial inflammation. Anti cN1A antibodies help. It is refractory to immunotherapy; offer supportive care and rehabilitation.

front: Core motor criteria for Parkinson disease (clinically established)
back: Bradykinesia plus either rest tremor or rigidity, supportive features present, no absolute exclusion criteria, and no red flags. Levodopa responsiveness and rest tremor support the diagnosis.

front: Earliest nonmotor features that can precede Parkinson motor signs by years
back: Hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, and depression. REM sleep behavior disorder carries the strongest risk of later phenotypic conversion to a synucleinopathy.

front: Most effective symptomatic drug for Parkinson disease
back: Levodopa combined with carbidopa, a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor that reduces nausea and orthostasis. Protein meals can compete for absorption and worsen wearing off.

front: Wearing off versus peak dose dyskinesia: management
back: Wearing off: shorten dosing intervals or add a COMT inhibitor, MAO B inhibitor, or agonist. Peak dose dyskinesia: reduce the individual levodopa dose or add amantadine. Deep brain stimulation helps both.

front: Dopamine agonist adverse effects to remember
back: Impulse control disorders, daytime sleep attacks, leg edema, hallucinations, and orthostasis. Ask about compulsive shopping, hypersexuality, and binge eating at every visit, and taper the agonist if they appear.
Block peripheral levodopa breakdown to prolong its effect and reduce wearing off. They are only useful with levodopa. Typical adverse effects: dyskinesia, orange urine, and diarrhea.

front: Good candidate for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson disease
back: A levodopa responsive patient with disabling fluctuations or dyskinesia, or tremor refractory to drugs, with intact cognition and no significant psychiatric disease. Targets are subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna.

First reduce anticholinergics, amantadine, and agonists, and look for infection. If antipsychotic is needed use pimavanserin, quetiapine, or clozapine. Avoid haloperidol and risperidone, which worsen parkinsonism.

front: Orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson disease: treatment
back: Stop offending drugs, increase fluids and salt, use compression stockings and head up sleeping. Add fludrocortisone, midodrine, or droxidopa if needed. Watch for supine hypertension.

front: Most common genetic cause of Parkinson disease in clinical practice
back: LRRK2 mutations (autosomal dominant, especially G2019S) and GBA variants, a risk factor with earlier onset and faster cognitive decline. Parkin mutations cause young onset recessive disease with slow progression.

Poor levodopa response with early severe dysautonomia, cerebellar signs in MSA C, or parkinsonism in MSA P. Hot cross bun sign and putaminal rim changes on MRI. Stridor and REM behavior disorder are common.
Early falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (down gaze first), axial rigidity, and frontal dysfunction. MRI shows midbrain atrophy with the hummingbird sign. Tau pathology, poor levodopa response.

Asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb phenomenon, and myoclonus, with asymmetric parietal atrophy. Levodopa response is poor. Pathology is often a tau disorder but may be Alzheimer disease.

front: Dementia with Lewy bodies versus Parkinson disease dementia
back: In Lewy body dementia cognitive impairment appears before or within one year of parkinsonism. Core features: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM behavior disorder. Avoid neuroleptic sensitivity reactions.

front: Treatment of cognitive and psychiatric symptoms in Lewy body dementia
back: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) help cognition and hallucinations. Use quetiapine or pimavanserin cautiously if an antipsychotic is unavoidable. Avoid typical antipsychotics because of severe sensitivity.
Lower body predominant parkinsonism with gait impairment, little tremor, and poor levodopa response. MRI shows extensive subcortical white matter or basal ganglia infarcts.

Usually symmetric, subacute, caused by dopamine blockers such as metoclopramide, antipsychotics, and prochlorperazine. Resolves over weeks to months after withdrawal. Persistence suggests unmasked Parkinson disease.

front: Normal pressure hydrocephalus triad and test
back: Magnetic gait first, then cognitive slowing and urinary urgency, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy. Large volume lumbar puncture with gait improvement predicts response to shunting.
Propranolol or primidone. Topiramate is second line. Refractory disabling tremor may respond to thalamic (Vim) deep brain stimulation or MR guided focused ultrasound, usually done unilaterally.

Essential tremor is bilateral, postural and kinetic, often familial, improves with a small dose of propranolol, and shows no bradykinesia. Parkinson tremor is asymmetric at rest, with bradykinesia and rigidity.

Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance, a GAG deletion, causing early limb onset generalized dystonia in childhood. Treatment includes anticholinergics, and deep brain stimulation of globus pallidus interna.
Childhood onset leg dystonia with diurnal fluctuation, worse late in the day, from GCH1 mutations. Dramatic and sustained response to small doses of levodopa.

front: Botulinum toxin: best indications in movement disorders
back: First line for cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, and focal dystonias such as writer cramp and spasmodic dysphonia. Repeat injections every three months. Adverse effects: dysphagia and weakness of nearby muscles.
Low ceruloplasmin, high 24 hour urinary copper, Kayser Fleischer rings, and hepatic involvement in a patient under 40 with movement disorder or psychiatric signs. ATP7B mutation, autosomal recessive.
Chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc to block intestinal copper absorption. Zinc is preferred for maintenance and presymptomatic patients. Avoid high copper foods, and screen siblings.
Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4, with anticipation especially through paternal transmission. Full penetrance at 40 or more repeats. Caudate atrophy on imaging.

VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) reduce chorea but can worsen depression and suicidality. Monitor mood closely. Antipsychotics are used when psychosis or irritability coexist.

Autoimmune complication of group A streptococcal infection, a major Jones criterion, in children, often with emotional lability. Treat with antibiotic prophylaxis, and valproate or carbamazepine for severe chorea.

Withdraw or switch the offending dopamine blocker if possible, and use a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine). Anticholinergics can worsen it. Typical features: orobuccolingual movements after months of antipsychotics.
Multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for over one year, onset before age 18. Comorbid ADHD and obsessive compulsive disorder are common.
Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics is first line. Alpha agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) are first drugs, then VMAT2 inhibitors or aripiprazole for severe tics.

Cortical myoclonus responds to levetiracetam, valproate, and piracetam. Subcortical myoclonus, such as myoclonus dystonia, may respond to clonazepam. Lance Adams syndrome is action myoclonus after hypoxic injury.

Fluctuating axial rigidity with painful spasms triggered by startle, with anti GAD65 antibodies in most. Treat with benzodiazepines (diazepam) and baclofen, then immunotherapy. Association with diabetes and thyroiditis.
Violent proximal flinging of contralateral limbs from a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus, often an infarct. Treat with dopamine blockers or VMAT2 inhibitors. It usually improves with time.

GAA trinucleotide expansion in frataxin (FXN), autosomal recessive, onset before 25. Features: areflexia, loss of proprioception, Babinski signs, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, diabetes. Omaveloxolone is approved.

Premutation CGG repeat (55 to 200) in FMR1, older men with intention tremor, ataxia, and cognitive decline. MRI shows middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) hyperintensity. Female carriers may have premature ovarian failure.

front: Restless legs syndrome: first treatment steps
back: Check ferritin and give iron if ferritin is 75 or below. Alpha 2 delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) are now preferred over dopamine agonists, which risk augmentation. Remove aggravators such as antihistamines and antidepressants.

Distractibility, entrainment of tremor, variability, sudden onset, and give way weakness. Diagnose on positive signs, not exclusion. Treatment is clear explanation plus physiotherapy and psychological therapy.

At least two of four CNS regions (periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) with one or more T2 lesions. Dissemination in time can be shown by new lesions or by CSF oligoclonal bands.

front: Typical MRI features of multiple sclerosis
back: Ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), juxtacortical and infratentorial lesions, short segment cord lesions, and the central vein sign. Gadolinium enhancement shows active lesions.

Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (under 50 cells), normal or mildly raised protein, and oligoclonal bands unique to CSF with elevated IgG index. Very high cell counts or protein suggest another diagnosis.

front: Primary progressive MS versus relapsing MS: differences
back: Primary progressive disease, about 10 to 15 percent, starts later with equal sex ratio and progressive myelopathy. Relapsing disease occurs mostly in young women. Ocrelizumab is approved for both.

Cortical gray matter syndromes, complete cord lesions over three segments, normal MRI with long course, fever, systemic features, or progressive disease from onset in young patients. Consider NMOSD, MOGAD, vasculitis, and sarcoid.

Relapses decrease in the third trimester and rise in the first three months postpartum. Most disease modifying drugs are stopped before conception, with glatiramer and some others used selectively. Breastfeeding is generally encouraged.
High dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3 to 5 days, or equivalent oral dosing. Plasma exchange is used for severe relapses not responding to steroids.

Risk rises with positive anti JC virus antibody index, treatment over two years, and prior immunosuppression. Index below 0.9 means low risk. Monitor MRI regularly. Natalizumab is an alpha 4 integrin antagonist.

front: Anti CD20 therapies in multiple sclerosis
back: Ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and ublituximab deplete B cells and are highly effective. Risks: infusion reactions, infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, and a poor vaccine response. Check hepatitis B status before starting.

front: Fingolimod, siponimod, and ozanimod: key cautions
back: Sphingosine 1 phosphate receptor modulators cause first dose bradycardia, macular edema, and lymphopenia. Do ECG and eye examination before starting. Fingolimod withdrawal may cause severe rebound.

front: Interferon beta and glatiramer: adverse effects
back: Interferon beta: flu like symptoms, injection site reactions, liver enzyme elevation, and neutralizing antibodies. Glatiramer: injection site lipoatrophy and a transient chest tightness reaction. Neither raises PML risk.
Teriflunomide: hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity, with accelerated elimination by cholestyramine. Cladribine: lymphopenia, malignancy risk, and teratogenicity, given as two short yearly courses.

front: Symptomatic MS drugs: spasticity, fatigue, walking
back: Baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity, dalfampridine to improve walking speed (avoid with seizures or renal impairment), and modafinil or amantadine for fatigue. Cooling can help heat sensitivity.
Aquaporin 4 IgG, an astrocytopathy, causes longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (three or more segments), severe optic neuritis, and area postrema syndrome with intractable vomiting.

Satralizumab (IL 6 receptor), inebilizumab (CD19), eculizumab or ravulizumab (complement C5), and rituximab. Acute attacks get steroids, then plasma exchange early. Avoid interferon beta and natalizumab, which can worsen NMOSD.
Optic neuritis with prominent disc swelling and perineural enhancement, ADEM in children, and myelitis involving the conus. Often a good recovery, with relapses in some patients.

front: ADEM versus first episode of MS
back: ADEM is monophasic, with encephalopathy and polyfocal deficits after infection or vaccination, mostly in children, with large fluffy lesions. Treat with high dose steroids, then IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange if refractory.

front: Optic neuritis: Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial lessons
back: Intravenous methylprednisolone speeds recovery but does not change final acuity. Oral prednisone alone increased recurrence. An abnormal brain MRI predicts a higher risk of later MS.
Large lesion over 2 cm with mass effect and open ring enhancement that can mimic tumor or abscess. Biopsy shows macrophages and reactive astrocytes. Treat with steroids, with a risk of later MS.

front: Balo concentric sclerosis and Marburg variant
back: Balo shows alternating rings of demyelination and preserved myelin on MRI. Marburg is a fulminant, often fatal, monophasic demyelinating disease. Both are treated with high dose steroids and plasma exchange.

front: Anti NMDA receptor encephalitis: presentation and tumor
back: Young women with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and hypoventilation. Look for ovarian teratoma by pelvic imaging. CSF antibody testing is more sensitive than serum.

Older men with limbic encephalitis, faciobrachial dystonic seizures, and hyponatremia. Treat with immunotherapy, as antiseizure drugs respond poorly. Tumor association is uncommon, but thymoma can occur.

front: Anti Hu (ANNA 1) and anti Yo (PCA 1): tumors
back: Anti Hu: small cell lung cancer, with encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy. Anti Yo: ovarian and breast cancer, with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration. Both are intracellular antigens with poor response to immunotherapy.

front: CASPR2 and GABA B receptor antibodies
back: CASPR2: neuromyotonia, Morvan syndrome, and limbic encephalitis, with thymoma. GABA B: limbic encephalitis with prominent early seizures, and small cell lung cancer in many cases.

front: Empiric therapy for adult bacterial meningitis
back: Vancomycin plus a third generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), with ampicillin added over age 50 or when immunocompromised to cover Listeria. Give dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose, mainly for pneumococcus.

front: Herpes simplex encephalitis: diagnosis and treatment
back: Fever, behavior change, and seizures with temporal lobe lesions. CSF HSV PCR confirms it. Start intravenous acyclovir immediately, before results, for 14 to 21 days.

front: Cryptococcal meningitis: key tests and treatment
back: CSF cryptococcal antigen is highly sensitive and the opening pressure is often raised. Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole. Repeat lumbar punctures reduce raised pressure.

Taenia solium cysts cause seizures, with a scolex in a cyst on MRI. Viable cysts get albendazole with or without praziquantel plus corticosteroids, and antiseizure drugs. Treat hydrocephalus surgically first.

CSF VDRL is specific but insensitive, and a reactive serum treponemal test is required. Treatment is intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days. Argyll Robertson pupils and tabes dorsalis are classic.

front: Cerebral toxoplasmosis versus primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS
back: Toxoplasmosis shows multiple ring enhancing lesions with positive serology, and responds to pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine within two weeks. Lymphoma is typically a single periventricular lesion with EBV in CSF.

Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus. MRI shows cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion. CSF 14 3 3 and RT QuIC are supportive, and periodic sharp wave complexes appear on EEG.

front: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: cause and diagnosis
back: JC virus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients, with asymmetric subcortical white matter lesions and no enhancement or mass effect. Diagnose by CSF JC virus PCR. Restore immunity, with no effective antiviral.

front: Migraine without aura: ICHD criteria in brief
back: At least five attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours untreated, with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate or severe, worse with activity, plus nausea or both photophobia and phonophobia.

front: Typical migraine aura: duration and features
back: Fully reversible visual, sensory, or speech symptoms that spread gradually over 5 minutes or more, with each symptom lasting 5 to 60 minutes. Headache usually follows within 60 minutes.
Coronary disease, prior stroke or TIA, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic or brainstem aura migraine, and use within 24 hours of an ergot. Serotonin 1B/1D agonists cause vasoconstriction.
Oral CGRP receptor antagonists with no vasoconstriction, so usable in patients with vascular risk. Rimegepant also has a preventive indication. Nausea and somnolence are the usual adverse effects.
Ditan acting on the serotonin 1F receptor, with no vasoconstriction. Causes dizziness and sedation, so patients must not drive for at least 8 hours after a dose.
Erenumab targets the CGRP receptor; fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and eptinezumab bind the CGRP ligand. Constipation and hypertension are noted with erenumab. Used when two oral preventives fail.
Propranolol or metoprolol, topiramate, and amitriptyline or venlafaxine are guideline level choices. Divalproex is effective but avoided in women of childbearing potential because of teratogenicity.

Approved only for chronic migraine, defined as 15 or more headache days per month with 8 or more migrainous. Injected every 12 weeks at 31 sites. Not effective for episodic migraine or tension type headache.
Headache on 15 or more days per month with triptans, ergots, or combination analgesics used 10 or more days per month, or simple analgesics 15 or more days. Treat by withdrawal plus a preventive.
Most migraine improves in the second and third trimesters. Acetaminophen is first line acute therapy; sumatriptan is considered reasonable if needed. Avoid valproate, topiramate, and ergots.
Familial forms: CACNA1A (FHM1), ATP1A2 (FHM2), SCN1A (FHM3). Aura includes fully reversible motor weakness. Avoid triptans; treat with preventives such as verapamil or acetazolamide.

front: Cluster headache: features and acute treatment
back: Strictly unilateral orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, up to 8 per day, with ipsilateral autonomic signs and restlessness. Treat with 100 percent oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min or subcutaneous sumatriptan.

Verapamil is first line for prevention, with ECG monitoring for PR prolongation as doses rise. Prednisone is a short bridging therapy; lithium is an alternative. Check ECG before and after dose increases.

Paroxysmal hemicrania: shorter attacks of 2 to 30 minutes, more frequent (more than 5 per day), more common in women, and absolutely responsive to indomethacin. Cluster attacks are longer and do not respond.

Continuous unilateral headache with exacerbations, ipsilateral autonomic features, and complete response to indomethacin. Give gastric protection with indomethacin; it is the diagnostic therapeutic test.
Very brief stabbing unilateral attacks of 1 to 600 seconds with prominent conjunctival injection and tearing. Lamotrigine is first line; consider MRI to exclude a posterior fossa or pituitary lesion.

Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, neurologic deficit, sudden onset, onset after age 50, pattern change, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilledema, pregnancy, and painful eye with autonomic features all prompt imaging.

Noncontrast head CT within 6 hours of onset is highly sensitive for subarachnoid hemorrhage. If negative, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or CT angiography follows. Consider RCVS and dissection as well.

Recurrent thunderclap headaches with segmental vasoconstriction that resolves in about 3 months. Triggers are vasoactive drugs, postpartum state, and exertion. Calcium channel blockers are used; avoid steroids, which worsen outcome.

front: Giant cell arteritis: action before biopsy
back: Age over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, high ESR or CRP. Start high dose prednisone immediately to prevent blindness; do not wait for temporal artery biopsy, which stays positive for weeks.

Opening pressure above 25 cm water with normal imaging and CSF content. Weight loss and acetazolamide first line; for severe or progressive visual loss, optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting.

Orthostatic headache with low opening pressure and MRI showing diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging, and subdural collections. Bed rest and hydration first; epidural blood patch if persistent.

front: Trigeminal neuralgia: first line and next step
back: Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine first line (check HLA B*1502 in patients of Asian ancestry and sodium). Obtain MRI to look for vascular compression or demyelination; microvascular decompression for refractory cases.

Type 1: cataplexy or CSF hypocretin 1 at or below 110 pg/mL, with loss of hypocretin neurons. Type 2: no cataplexy and normal hypocretin. Both show mean sleep latency 8 minutes or less and two SOREMPs on MSLT.

front: Sleep study done before an MSLT
back: Overnight polysomnography the night before, with at least 6 hours of sleep, to exclude sleep apnea and insufficient sleep. Stop REM suppressing antidepressants for about two weeks if safe.

Excessive sleepiness: modafinil, armodafinil, solriamfetol, pitolisant, or oxybates. Cataplexy: sodium oxybate, pitolisant, venlafaxine, or fluoxetine. Abrupt antidepressant withdrawal can trigger status cataplecticus.

Dream enactment with REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography. Strongly predicts synucleinopathy (Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, MSA). Treat with melatonin or clonazepam and secure the bedroom.

Obstructive: effort without airflow, treat with CPAP. Central: no effort or airflow, linked to heart failure, opioids, and stroke. Cheyne Stokes pattern and adaptive servo ventilation caution when ejection fraction is low.

Sleepwalking, night terrors, and confusional arousal arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, with amnesia. Treat triggers such as sleep deprivation and apnea; safety measures are key.
Adolescents with late sleep onset and late waking but normal sleep when allowed their own schedule. Treat with timed evening low dose melatonin and morning bright light.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (stimulus control, sleep restriction) is first line. Pharmacologic options include short term z drugs, low dose doxepin, or orexin antagonists; avoid chronic benzodiazepines.

Gabapentinoids, SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine), and tricyclics (nortriptyline, amitriptyline). Topical lidocaine or capsaicin for focal pain. Avoid tricyclics in older adults with cardiac disease or cognitive impairment.

front: Complex regional pain syndrome: Budapest criteria
back: Continuing disproportionate pain after an injury plus sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor or edema, and motor or trophic changes. Treat with early physical therapy; bisphosphonates, steroids, and neuromodulation are options.
Drop of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. Neurogenic types show a blunted heart rate rise, under 0.5 beats per minute per mm Hg of systolic fall.

Pure autonomic failure: low supine norepinephrine and a lack of CNS features, though may precede Lewy disease. MSA: preserved norepinephrine, with parkinsonism or cerebellar signs, stridor, and urinary retention.
Montreal Cognitive Assessment is scored out of 30, with 26 or above normal; add one point if education is 12 years or less. More sensitive than the MMSE for MCI and executive dysfunction.

Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, altered arousal; look for a medical trigger. Dementia: insidious, stable attention until late, clear consciousness. Delirium may be superimposed on dementia.

B12 (with methylmalonic acid if borderline), TSH, CBC, metabolic panel, and structural brain imaging. Add HIV and syphilis testing when risk factors exist; screen for depression and review medications.
Amnestic MCI (memory loss) most often progresses to Alzheimer disease at roughly 10 to 15 percent per year. Nonamnestic types affecting language or executive function point toward other dementias.

Depressive cognitive complaint: patient emphasizes deficits, answers don't know, effort is poor, and mood symptoms came first. Dementia patients minimize deficits and confabulate. Treat depression and reassess.

Extracellular beta amyloid plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, beginning in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus. Biomarkers: low CSF amyloid beta 42, high phospho tau, positive amyloid PET.

Early onset autosomal dominant: APP, PSEN1 (most common), PSEN2. APOE e4 is the main risk allele for late onset disease; e2 is protective. Down syndrome carries extra APP and early Alzheimer pathology.
Lecanemab and donanemab slow decline in early Alzheimer disease with confirmed amyloid. ARIA (edema or hemorrhage) risk is highest in APOE e4 homozygotes; serial MRI monitoring is required.

Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine for mild to moderate disease; adverse effects are nausea, bradycardia, syncope, and vivid dreams. Memantine, an NMDA antagonist, is added for moderate to severe disease.

Early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, and hyperorality, with relatively preserved memory. Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Genes: C9orf72, MAPT, GRN. Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors.

front: Dementia with Lewy bodies core features
back: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism. If dementia precedes parkinsonism by a year or less, it is DLB. Avoid typical antipsychotics.

front: Neuroleptic sensitivity in Lewy body disease
back: Haloperidol and other D2 blockers can cause severe rigidity and decline. If antipsychotic is needed use low dose quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin; rivastigmine can treat hallucinations.

Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and ataxia. MRI diffusion restriction in cortical ribbon and basal ganglia; CSF 14 3 3 protein, RT-QuIC highly specific; periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG.

Subacute cognitive decline with seizures or psychiatric features: send CSF and serum for autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and treat with steroids, IVIG, or plasma exchange. Check for underlying tumor.

Stepwise or subcortical pattern with executive slowing, gait disturbance, and white matter disease. Manage blood pressure, lipids, and antithrombotic therapy. CADASIL (NOTCH3) causes migraine with aura and early strokes.

Impaired word retrieval and sentence repetition with intact motor speech and grammar; usually underlying Alzheimer pathology. Semantic variant shows loss of word meaning; nonfluent variant shows agrammatism and apraxia of speech.
Anterior temporal atrophy, impaired confrontation naming and single word comprehension, surface dyslexia. Fluent but empty speech; usually TDP 43 pathology.

Delusion that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor. Seen in dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer disease, and schizophrenia; thought to involve disconnection of face recognition from emotional familiarity.

Bilateral anterior temporal and amygdala damage causing hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia, and hypermetamorphosis. Seen with herpes encephalitis, trauma, and frontotemporal dementia.
Bilateral parieto occipital lesions: simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and oculomotor apraxia. Classic in posterior cortical atrophy and watershed infarction.

Anosognosia: unawareness of deficit, classically left hemiplegia from right parietal stroke. Anton syndrome: denial of blindness from bilateral occipital lesions, with confabulated visual description.
Dorsolateral: executive dysfunction and perseveration. Orbitofrontal: disinhibition and impulsivity. Medial or anterior cingulate: apathy and abulia, with akinetic mutism if bilateral.

Anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation after untreated Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Damage to mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus. Give thiamine before glucose.
Dominant angular gyrus lesion: acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left right confusion.

Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, ataxia, confusion, seizures. Risk rises with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazides. Chronic use causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and hypothyroidism; severe toxicity needs dialysis.

front: Valproate for migraine prophylaxis: which adverse effects limit its use?
back: Teratogenicity (neural tube defects, lower IQ), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, tremor, weight gain, and thrombocytopenia. Avoid in mitochondrial POLG disease.
