Stevens Johnson syndrome risk rises with rapid titration and with valproate co administration, which doubles its level. Titrate slowly; stop at the first sign of rash with mucosal involvement.
Acute dystonia: anticholinergic or benztropine. Akathisia: propranolol or lower dose. Tardive dyskinesia: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine). Parkinsonism: lower dose or switch agent.
Serotonin syndrome: hours onset, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, treated with cyproheptadine. NMS: days onset, lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high CK, treated with dantrolene or bromocriptine.

Hyponatremia from SIADH (especially older adults), bleeding risk, sexual dysfunction, QT prolongation with citalopram, and discontinuation syndrome. Paroxetine has strongest anticholinergic effect and shortest half life.
Lowers the seizure threshold, so avoid in epilepsy, eating disorders, and abrupt sedative withdrawal. Useful for smoking cessation and depression without sexual dysfunction.

Hoover sign for leg weakness, give way weakness, tremor entrainment, and functional gait. Diagnosis rests on positive findings, not exclusion. First line treatment is explanation plus physiotherapy and CBT.
Long duration, eye closure, side to side head movement, asynchronous thrashing, and recall. Video EEG is the gold standard; serum prolactin is not reliable. Treat with CBT.
Signs: mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, stupor or excitement. Give lorazepam challenge; ECT if refractory or malignant. Distinguish from NMS and avoid antipsychotics early.

front: Suicide risk assessment in neurologic disease
back: Elevated in epilepsy, Huntington disease, multiple sclerosis, and after stroke or TBI. Ask directly about ideation, plan, and access to means; asking does not increase risk. Prior attempt is the strongest predictor.

front: Bitemporal hemianopia: lesion site and classic cause
back: Optic chiasm compression crossing nasal retinal fibers, classically from a pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, or suprasellar meningioma. Superior quadrant loss usually points to a lesion pressing from below, such as a pituitary tumor.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Right homonymous superior quadrantanopia (pie in the sky): where is the lesion?
back: Left temporal lobe lesion involving Meyer loop, which carries inferior retinal (upper field) fibers. Parietal lesions of the superior optic radiation cause inferior quadrantanopia (pie on the floor).
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing: localization
back: Occipital cortex lesion, typically a posterior cerebral artery stroke, with preserved central vision because of dual blood supply from the middle cerebral artery to the occipital pole.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Relative afferent pupillary defect: what does it show?
back: Unilateral or asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal disease. On the swinging flashlight test the affected pupil dilates when light moves to it. Cataract and refractive error do not cause it.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light (light near dissociation), classically neurosyphilis. Diagnose with serum treponemal testing and CSF analysis, treat with intravenous penicillin G.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Horner syndrome: triad and pharmacologic localization
back: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Apraclonidine reverses the anisocoria (denervation supersensitivity). Hydroxyamphetamine testing separates preganglionic from postganglionic lesions. Painful Horner syndrome with neck pain suggests carotid dissection.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Large pupil with a poor light response and slow tonic constriction to near, from ciliary ganglion damage. Dilute pilocarpine causes constriction (supersensitivity). Often associated with absent knee and ankle reflexes.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Third nerve palsy: pupil involvement and what it implies
back: A dilated, poorly reactive pupil with a down and out eye suggests compression, especially a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, and needs urgent vascular imaging. Pupil sparing suggests ischemic microvascular disease from diabetes or hypertension.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Papilledema versus idiopathic intracranial hypertension: first treatment
back: Papilledema is disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure. In IIH, image to exclude mass and venous thrombosis, confirm opening pressure above 25 cm water, start acetazolamide and weight loss, and consider optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunt for failing vision.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: lesion, finding, and classic association
back: Medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causing failed adduction on the side of the lesion with abducting nystagmus in the other eye. Bilateral in multiple sclerosis, unilateral in brainstem stroke.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: diagnosis and treatment
back: Brief vertigo triggered by head position with torsional upbeating nystagmus on the Dix Hallpike maneuver, usually posterior canal. Treat with the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver, not vestibular suppressants.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: HINTS exam findings that suggest stroke in acute vestibular syndrome
back: Normal head impulse test, direction changing gaze evoked nystagmus, or skew deviation on test of skew. Any one points to central cause. It applies only to continuous vertigo with nystagmus, not to episodic dizziness.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Both cause acute continuous vertigo with unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, abnormal head impulse, and no central signs. Labyrinthitis adds hearing loss and tinnitus. Treat briefly with vestibular suppressants, early corticosteroids, and early mobilization.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Meniere disease: triad and first line management
back: Episodic vertigo lasting twenty minutes to hours, fluctuating low frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness (endolymphatic hydrops). Start with sodium restriction and diuretics, then consider intratympanic therapy for refractory cases.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Vertigo and oscillopsia triggered by loud sounds (Tullio) or pressure changes, autophonia, and conductive hearing loss with normal middle ear. Confirm with high resolution temporal bone CT, and lower thresholds on vestibular evoked myogenic potentials.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, with loss of speech discrimination. Gadolinium MRI shows an enhancing cerebellopontine angle mass extending into the internal auditory canal. Bilateral tumors define neurofibromatosis type 2.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Clinical diagnosis with normal routine imaging. Brief initial rest, then gradual stepwise return to school and sport. Most recover within weeks. A second impact during recovery risks prolonged symptoms. Avoid return to play while symptomatic.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Glasgow Coma Scale ranges for traumatic brain injury severity
back: Mild is 13 to 15, moderate is 9 to 12, severe is 8 or less. Severe injury needs airway protection, head elevation, avoidance of hypotension and hypoxia, and intracranial pressure management.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Epidural versus subdural hematoma on CT
back: Epidural is biconvex (lens shaped), does not cross sutures, and follows arterial injury of the middle meningeal artery with a lucid interval. Subdural is crescentic, crosses sutures, and follows bridging vein tear.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Diffuse axonal injury: imaging and mechanism
back: Rotational acceleration and deceleration shear axons, causing immediate coma with often normal early CT. MRI with susceptibility weighted sequences shows microhemorrhages at gray white junction, corpus callosum, and dorsolateral brainstem.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Hemicord lesion: ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception below the level, contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few segments lower. Penetrating trauma and MS are common causes.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Anterior cord syndrome versus central cord syndrome
back: Anterior cord: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal column function, from anterior spinal artery infarction. Central cord: arms weaker than legs after hyperextension injury in a patient with cervical stenosis.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Cape distribution dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, touch and vibration spared), hand weakness, and areflexia in the arms. Associated with Chiari I malformation. MRI shows a cervical cord cavity.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Chiari I malformation: definition and surgical indication
back: Cerebellar tonsils descend at least 5 mm below the foramen magnum. Causes cough headache, syringomyelia, and lower cranial signs. Posterior fossa decompression is indicated for progressive deficits or syrinx, not for asymptomatic findings.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Spinal cord compression in cancer: next best step
back: Back pain with weakness or sensory level in a patient with known malignancy needs immediate whole spine MRI and high dose dexamethasone, followed by urgent radiation therapy or surgical decompression, depending on stability and tumor type.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: IDH mutant versus IDH wild type glioma
back: IDH mutation marks lower grade astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma with a better prognosis. Oligodendroglioma also needs 1p19q codeletion. IDH wild type diffuse glioma in an adult behaves as glioblastoma.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Maximal safe resection, then radiation with concurrent temozolomide, followed by adjuvant temozolomide. MGMT promoter methylation predicts better response to temozolomide. Median survival remains about fifteen months.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Extra axial dural based enhancing mass with a dural tail. Asymptomatic small lesions are observed. Symptomatic or growing tumors are resected or irradiated. Associated with prior cranial radiation and neurofibromatosis type 2.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Primary CNS lymphoma: features and treatment
back: Usually diffuse large B cell. Periventricular homogeneously enhancing lesions, often in immunocompromised patients. Avoid steroids before biopsy because tumors may vanish. Treat with high dose methotrexate based chemotherapy.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell, and colon. Melanoma, renal cell, and choriocarcinoma tend to bleed. Treat with dexamethasone for edema, and stereotactic radiosurgery for limited lesions, surgery for a large single symptomatic lesion.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Multifocal cranial nerve, radicular, and cerebral signs in cancer patients. MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement. CSF cytology confirms but may need repeat sampling. CSF shows high protein and low glucose.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Prolactinoma is the most common functional adenoma. First line treatment is a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline, even for large tumors with visual loss. Surgery is for failure or intolerance.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, and hypopituitarism from hemorrhage into an adenoma. Give intravenous hydrocortisone for adrenal insufficiency, and consider urgent transsphenoidal decompression for deficits.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Dexamethasone adverse effects in neuro oncology
back: Hyperglycemia, proximal steroid myopathy, insomnia, mood change, gastric irritation, and opportunistic infection such as Pneumocystis pneumonia with prolonged use. Use the lowest effective dose and taper once edema is controlled.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Osmotic demyelination syndrome: cause and presentation
back: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, more than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours, causes quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and locked in state days later. Pontine T2 hyperintensity on MRI. Prevention is key.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Asterixis, confusion, and elevated ammonia in liver disease. Identify precipitants such as infection, bleeding, or constipation. Treat with lactulose, add rifaximin for recurrence prevention.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and gait ataxia from thiamine deficiency in malnutrition. Give intravenous thiamine before or with glucose, at high doses, because glucose can precipitate or worsen the syndrome.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes dorsal column and corticospinal tract degeneration with paresthesias, sensory ataxia, spasticity, and macrocytic anemia. Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm. Treat with parenteral B12. Folate alone can worsen neurologic disease.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Mimics B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia and spastic gait, plus anemia and neutropenia. Causes include gastric surgery and excess zinc intake. Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin. Replace copper and stop zinc.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Spinocerebellar ataxia, areflexia, and loss of proprioception, seen in fat malabsorption and abetalipoproteinemia. Resembles Friedreich ataxia. Treat with high dose vitamin E.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Episodes of abdominal pain, psychiatric symptoms, hyponatremia, and motor neuropathy triggered by drugs, fasting, or hormones. Urine porphobilinogen is raised during attacks. Treat with intravenous hemin and glucose, and avoid triggers.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Wilson disease: neurologic features and diagnosis
back: Young patient with dystonia, tremor, parkinsonism, and psychiatric change, with Kayser Fleischer rings. Low ceruloplasmin, high 24 hour urine copper. Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation. Treat with chelation or zinc.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Lethargy, confusion, weakness, and depression from malignancy or hyperparathyroidism. Treat with intravenous fluids, then bisphosphonate. Severe cases may cause coma.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Carbon monoxide poisoning: imaging and treatment
back: Headache, nausea, and confusion in winter heating exposure with cherry red appearance rarely seen. Carboxyhemoglobin confirms. Give 100 percent oxygen. MRI shows globus pallidus lesions, with delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome weeks later.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Lead causes motor predominant neuropathy, classically wrist drop, with abdominal pain and anemia with basophilic stippling. Arsenic causes painful sensory neuropathy with Mees lines, skin changes, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Cholinergic crisis with miosis, bradycardia, salivation, and fasciculations from acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Treat with atropine for muscarinic effects and pralidoxime for nicotinic effects, plus decontamination.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: How do you tell serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome at the bedside?
back: Serotonin syndrome: onset within hours, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, treat with cyproheptadine. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: days, lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, raised creatine kinase, treat with dantrolene or bromocriptine.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Perioral numbness, tinnitus, and seizures, then cardiovascular collapse after nerve block injection. Treat with airway support, benzodiazepine for seizures, and intravenous lipid emulsion.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Cancer drug neurotoxicity: cisplatin versus vincristine versus ifosfamide
back: Cisplatin causes sensory ganglionopathy and ototoxicity. Vincristine causes length dependent neuropathy with autonomic features such as constipation. Ifosfamide causes an acute encephalopathy treated with methylene blue.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Huntington disease: gene, inheritance, and mechanism
back: CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4, autosomal dominant, with anticipation through paternal transmission. Chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive decline. Caudate atrophy on imaging. Repeats of 40 or more give full penetrance.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Trinucleotide repeat disorders: repeat type by disease
back: Fragile X: CGG. Huntington and spinocerebellar ataxias: CAG. Friedreich ataxia: GAA. Myotonic dystrophy type 1: CTG. Anticipation occurs in expanding repeats, with earlier and worse disease in later generations.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Maternal inheritance from mitochondrial DNA, with heteroplasmy explaining variable severity. Affected fathers do not transmit to children. Examples include MELAS, MERRF, and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Both involve chromosome 15q11 to q13. Loss of the maternal copy (UBE3A) causes Angelman: seizures, ataxia, happy demeanor, absent speech. Loss of the paternal copy causes Prader Willi: neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: MECP2 mutation, X linked dominant, mostly girls. Normal early development, then regression with loss of hand use, stereotyped hand wringing, acquired microcephaly, gait abnormality, and seizures.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: FMR1 CGG expansion over 200 with methylation. Intellectual disability, autism features, long face, large ears, macroorchidism. Premutation carriers risk tremor ataxia syndrome and primary ovarian insufficiency. Test by DNA analysis, not karyotype.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Genetic testing choice for a child with developmental delay
back: Chromosomal microarray is first tier testing for unexplained developmental delay, intellectual disability, or autism. Add fragile X testing, and consider exome sequencing when microarray is nondiagnostic.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: No social smile by 3 months, no sitting by 9 months, no walking by 18 months, no single words by 16 months, and no two word phrases by 24 months. Loss of previously acquired skills is regression and needs urgent evaluation.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Spastic diplegia: risk factor and lesion
back: Cerebral palsy form linked to prematurity, with periventricular leukomalacia on imaging. Legs affected more than arms. Dyskinetic cerebral palsy is linked to kernicterus and basal ganglia injury.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: Hypotonic infant: central versus peripheral clues
back: Central: normal or brisk reflexes, poor interaction, seizures, dysmorphism. Peripheral: absent reflexes, weakness with alert face, fasciculations. Spinal muscular atrophy shows tongue fasciculations with SMN1 deletion, and is treatable.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Cool term or near term infants with moderate to severe encephalopathy to 33 to 34 degrees Celsius for 72 hours, starting within 6 hours of birth. It reduces death and disability.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Arises from the germinal matrix, usually in the first days of life in infants under 32 weeks. Screen with cranial ultrasound. Grade 3 and 4 carry risk of posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus and cerebral palsy.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia deposits in basal ganglia, causing athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, and upgaze paralysis. Treat hyperbilirubinemia early with phototherapy and exchange transfusion.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Most common congenital infection. Microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, and chorioretinitis. Congenital toxoplasmosis shows diffuse calcifications and hydrocephalus. Treat symptomatic CMV with valganciclovir.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Folic acid before conception reduces neural tube defects. Associated with Chiari II malformation, hydrocephalus, and neurogenic bladder. Elevated maternal alpha fetoprotein screens. Surgical closure is performed early.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: NF1 gene, autosomal dominant: six or more café au lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, and sphenoid dysplasia. Surveillance is annual eye examinations in childhood.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: TSC1 or TSC2, mTOR pathway. Infantile spasms, hypomelanotic macules, cortical tubers, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, angiomyolipoma. Treat spasms with vigabatrin, and tumors with everolimus.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: Facial capillary malformation (nevus flammeus) in the V1 distribution with leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma, and hemiparesis. Imaging shows tram track calcification. Caused by somatic GNAQ mutation.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: ATM mutation, autosomal recessive. Progressive cerebellar ataxia from early childhood, ocular telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, elevated alpha fetoprotein, and lymphoma risk. Avoid unnecessary radiation exposure.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

back: ABCD1 mutation with very long chain fatty acid accumulation. Boys develop school age behavior decline and visual and gait loss with posterior white matter disease. Adrenal insufficiency occurs. Early hematopoietic stem cell transplant helps.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology

front: MOG antibody associated disease in children versus pediatric MS
back: MOGAD often presents as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis in young children, with large fluffy lesions and often a monophasic course. Pediatric MS shows relapses with periventricular lesions. Test serum MOG antibody.
area: Special senses, trauma, toxic, and child neurology
